Write a hiring brief that gets the right shortlist

For technical leaders: how to write a hiring brief that recruiters can act on, with testable must-haves, precise technical context and a clear offer.

  1. Home
  2. Insights
  3. Write a hiring brief that gets the right shortlist

24 November 2026 · 5 min read

  • Guide
  • Technical leaders
  • HR leaders

If the CVs you receive keep missing the point, the problem often starts before the search: in the brief. A brief is the specification for the search. Like any specification, a vague one produces something that matches the words and misses the intent.

A good brief takes an hour of the hiring manager’s time. It saves many more hours of interviews with people who were never going to fit.

Start from the work, not the job title

“Senior backend developer” or “automation engineer” describes thousands of different jobs. Start with what the person will actually do:

  • The problems they will own. “Reduce the release cycle of our payment service from monthly to weekly.” “Take over the PLC software of two packaging lines and lead the next retrofit.”
  • What they deliver in the first six to twelve months. Concrete results, not responsibilities.
  • Who they work with. Team size, who they report to, which other teams or customers they deal with.

A recruiter who understands the work can recognise a good candidate whose CV uses different words, and can rule out a candidate whose CV matches every keyword but whose experience doesn’t fit.

Separate must-haves from teachable skills

Most briefs list too many requirements. Every additional must-have shrinks the pool, and lists of ten “essential” skills usually describe a person who doesn’t exist.

Sort each requirement into one of three groups:

  1. Must-have on day one. Without it, the person can’t do the job in the first months. Keep this to a handful of items.
  2. Can be learned on the job. Useful, but your team can teach it in weeks.
  3. Nice to have. A bonus, never a reason to reject.

Then check that every must-have is testable. “Strong problem-solving skills” is not. “Has diagnosed intermittent faults on a production line from PLC and drive logs” is, and the technical interview can ask about it.

Be careful with years of experience. Five years of repeating the same work is not the same as five years of growing responsibility. Describe the level of autonomy you need instead: “designs a feature end to end and reviews others’ code”, or “commissions a line on site without supervision”.

Name the technical context precisely

Engineers judge a role by its context. So do good recruiters. Be specific about:

  • Technologies and standards, with versions or variants where they matter: “Siemens TIA Portal and S7-1500”, “Kubernetes in production on a managed cloud”, “IEC 62443 for industrial control systems”.
  • The state of the system: greenfield, a mature product, or legacy code that needs care.
  • Ways of working: code review, testing, on-call duty, travel to sites or customers, safety requirements on the shop floor.
  • Constraints: security clearance, language requirements, a professional registration where the role requires one.

Precise context also helps the candidate. Engineers who are not actively looking decide whether to talk to you based on what the work involves.

Say how you will assess candidates

Agree the selection process before the search starts, and write it into the brief:

  • which competences the technical interview will test, and who runs it;
  • the interview stages, their order and roughly how long each takes;
  • how quickly you will give feedback after each stage.

Slow feedback loses good candidates. If your team can only interview on certain days, say so now, so interviews can be planned around it.

Be clear about the offer

Candidates ask about the package, the contract and the way of working early, and they are right to. Include in the brief:

  • the salary range, or the rate for project work;
  • the contract type: permanent, or a project engagement with a defined scope and duration;
  • on site, hybrid or remote, and where the site is;
  • anything unusual, such as shifts, frequent travel or a relocation package.

A recruiter who can answer these questions in the first call keeps the right candidates interested and saves everyone time with the wrong ones.

Agree what a good shortlist looks like

Decide together what you expect to receive: a small number of candidates, each with a written assessment against the must-haves. Say what would make you reject a profile immediately, and what would make you want to meet someone even if they miss one requirement.

Then review the first profiles quickly and give specific feedback. “Too junior” helps less than “hasn’t led a commissioning on site, which this role needs from month two”. The first round of feedback calibrates the rest of the search.

A checklist for your next brief

  • The problems the person will own, and the results expected in their first year
  • Team, reporting line and main contacts
  • Must-haves (few, each testable), skills that can be learned, nice-to-haves
  • Technologies, standards and the state of the system
  • Ways of working, travel and constraints
  • Selection stages, interviewers and feedback times
  • Salary range or rate, contract type, work mode and location
  • What a good shortlist looks like, and what rules a candidate out

Keep the brief alive

A brief is not fixed once the search starts. If the first interviews show that a requirement matters less than you thought, or that a missing one matters more, update it and share the change. The search improves as soon as the specification does.

Our talent acquisition service starts every search from a brief agreed with HR and the hiring manager, including the competences to test. For a project peak or a gap that can’t wait, the same approach applies to a project brief for temporary staffing: scope, deliverables, competences and duration, agreed before the search starts.
